text.p: Forecasts of colder weather in the U.S. drove up oil prices overnight while while wheat stayed above the psychological $4 per bushel level.
However, copper slipped below $2,100 support ahead of inventory data expected to show more metal in warehouses and other metals joined the slided.
The CRB index, helped by firmer oil and grain prices, was up 1.80 at 245.58 in late trading.

LME copper prices crumbled below $2,100 support on Monday afternoon as spreads eased and ahead of inventory data expected to show more metal in exchange warehouses. Many of the other metals joined the slide with tin hitting fresh 19-month lows and nickel touching a new 26-month nadir. Three months copper ended the afternoon kerb at $2,081 per tonne, down $51 from Friday and only $1 off the low for the day. "I think we're going to see softer prices now that the tight December dates are mostly out of the way," said one senior floor trader.

The premium of cash over three months metal eased again after third Wednesday pricing went smoothly in the morning, disappointing some who had expected some volatility. It was last indicated at a $55 backwardation compared to a $100 backwardation on Friday. Floor traders said they expected LME inventories to rise again on Tuesday after a build of 7,225 tonnes on Friday. Several traders said they expected stocks to rise by 8,000-10,000 tonnes, although one trader thought they could increase as much as 12,000 tonnes.

Nickel dropped to its weakest since October 1994, as three months metal ended the kerb at its day's low of $6,510, a loss of $125. Technical analysts said the confirmed breach of $6,600 support, where it bottomed out on November 18, weakened the chart picture and made further falls to $6,400 likely.

Tin slipped to a low of $5,680, the lowest since May 12, 1995, but it edged up slightly by the end of the day to $5,685, a loss of $90. The market had been hit by fund liquidation recently and soft technicals, traders said.

Aluminium, however, ignored the weakness in the others and managed to gain $6 to $1,516 after exploring a low of $1,507. Zinc eased $8 to $1,045 and trade was light in lead, which finished indicated at $689/90, down slightly from $695 on Friday. Alloy was indicated at $1,357/60 versus $1,365.

New York precious metals futures ended lower Monday, but last week's support levels were still holding and volumes were very low. "Investors generally remain out of the market, but there has been talk that the recent lower prices have brought out some investment buyingin Asia in particular," CPM Group analyst Edward Kempf said. COMEX February gold closed down 50 cents at $369.90 an ounce after trading down to a session low at $369.10, a level still above the contract low at $367.70 seen on December 3. Spot gold in the bullion market was quoted $367.80/368.30, against the London Monday afternoon fix at $368.25, and the New York close Friday at $368.45/368.95.

World oil prices gained further ground on Monday as traders chose to focus on low heating oil stocks and cold weather forecasts rather than the first tanker loadings of Iraqi crude export. Together with Friday's sharp $1.00 a barrel rally, Monday's gains almost wiped out losses from a ferocious sell-off earlier last week sparked by the resumption of Iraqi exports. Industry-watchers said forecasts for cold weather and low heating oil stock levels should at least keep a floor under oil prices and could possibly push them even higher. In late trading on NYMEX, January cruce was up $1.08 a barrel at $25.55.

Better-than-expected export numbers in USDA's weekly export inspections report and cold weather in the U.S. winter wheat growing region boosted CBOT wheat futures to a higher close. But agronomists said the cold air probably will not cause much damage to the U.S. wheat crop, despite the lack of insulating snow cover in many regions. Wheat also was bolstered by a rumor Russia may be offered credit to buy 200,000 tonnes of wheat but talk also circulated that a Russian delegation's visit to Washington was cancelled. Wheat futures were unchanged to 7-3/4 cents per bushel higher, with December up 7-3/4 at $4.13-3/4.
